# What is the damage causing and caused by, a diesel run-on?

A "diesel run-on," often colloquially referred to as a "run-away" condition, describes a catastrophic failure mode where an engine continues to operate at high RPMs without driver input. This isn't merely fuel starvation or a limp-home mode; it is the uncontrolled injection of combustible material into the combustion chamber. In your 20-year-old Mercedes Sprinter, the specific symptom you describedâcombusting engine oil intended for lubricationâis the critical indicator that this event has already occurred.

The mechanism behind this phenomenon is distinct from standard fuel injector failure. A diesel run-on typically occurs when the control system governing the injection pumps or injectors loses the ability to cut off fuel delivery. In modern common-rail systems, this involves a loss of electrical signal or a mechanical seizure within the high-pressure pump. However, your specific scenario points toward a different root cause: oil intrusion into the air intake or turbocharger path.

When engine oil is drawn into the combustion chamber, it acts as an unregulated fuel source. Unlike diesel injection pumps which are timed by the ECU to deliver precise amounts of fuel at specific intervals, oil entering via a compromised seal (such as a worn crankshaft seal or a leaking turbo shaft seal) bypasses all metering logic. The engine management system detects a drop in cylinder pressure due to blow-by and may attempt to compensate, but it cannot account for the sudden influx of liquid lubricant acting as fuel. As this oil burns, temperatures rise rapidly, leading to the "run-on" sensation where the engine revs up uncontrollably before finally seizing or stalling out completely once the available combustible oil is depleted.

The damage caused by such an event is often more severe than initially assumed. The prevailing theory that you might be able to simply refill the oil and restart the engine is dangerous advice without a full diagnostic. Burning oil at high combustion temperatures leads to carbon buildup on piston rings, cylinder walls, and valves. More critically, the heat generated can warp pistons or damage the turbocharger turbine wheel, which rotates at speeds exceeding 100,000 RPM. If the turbo shaft seal failed, allowing oil into the intake, the centrifugal force generated by the spinning rotor likely already sheared the seal further, potentially causing metal-to-metal contact between the compressor and turbine wheels.

From a mechanical engineering perspective, the decision to "deliberately stall" versus turning the key off is significant. Turning an engine key off cuts ignition or fuel but leaves hydraulic pressure in the system momentarily. A deliberate stallâoften achieved by cutting power to the starter motor while the engine is cranking or engaging the parking brake aggressively if transmission neutral isn't possibleâcan sometimes limit the duration of the uncontrolled burn. However, once oil has been combusted, the thermal damage is often irreversible.

To prevent recurrence, the focus must be on sealing integrity rather than just fuel system diagnostics. You need to inspect the crankshaft rear main seal and the turbocharger shaft seals for wear or defects. Additionally, checking the Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) system is essential; a clogged PCV valve can create a vacuum leak that might draw oil vapors into the intake manifold if the seals are marginal.

If you attempt to run the vehicle again with fresh oil without addressing the underlying seal failure or inspecting the turbocharger internals, you risk immediate catastrophic seizure of the crankshaft due to the same lubrication starvation conditions that caused the initial failure. The engine is likely salvageable only if a teardown reveals no scored cylinder walls or melted pistons, which are common side effects of burning significant quantities of oil under high load.
